They were taken before rumors of an affair with President John F. Kennedy began to circulate, and before her mental breakdowns became public. They were taken before the beautiful actress’s mysterious overdose, which led to her death at age 36.

In a collection discovered last month by Life.com, previously unpublished photographs of Monroe reveal a softer, more innocent 24-year-old starlet on the cusp of fame, captured during a more peaceful period before her celebrity reached its peak.

Her flawless face appears natural, with minimal makeup—an unusual look for a star who was often glamorized in photo shoots with lipstick, designer dresses and expensive jewelry.

Monday would have marked Monroe’s 83rd birthday.

In one photograph, the young Monroe reclines blissfully on a park bench, reading—an image that Life.com editors believe was taken at Griffith Park in Los Angeles, California. In another, she appears serene as she perches barefoot on a bridge.

The 1950 shoot was conducted by *Life* photographer Ed Clark. It presents a side of Monroe rarely seen by the American public.

“She hasn’t really exploded as a star; yet she was on the brink of something big,” said Dawnie Walton, deputy editor of Life.com, a website that houses more than 7 million *Life* magazine photographs. The site launched in March. “I was amazed looking at her face. Although she looks very innocent, there is something very ... sexy.”

Last month, Walton came across the rare photographs while searching through the company’s digital photo archives. Apparently, no one at Life.com even knew they had been taken.

After investigating the images, Walton said she found very few notes left on the negatives. She believes the photographs were likely taken for a cover shoot that was never used. Monroe appeared on her first *Life* magazine cover in 1952.

See some of the previously unpublished photos of Monroe » .

“It just got lost and stowed away,” Walton said. “It was just ... somewhere in a warehouse in New Jersey.”

At the time the photographs were taken, Monroe had landed her first modest breakout role, playing a mistress in *The Asphalt Jungle*. She was better known then as a model, though she had already appeared in a handful of film cameos.

Photographer Ed Clark told the *Sarasota Herald-Tribune* that a friend at 20th Century Fox had alerted him that the studio had just signed “a hot tomato.”

“She was unknown then, so I was able to spend a lot of time shooting her,” Clark said. “We’d go out to Griffith Park and she’d read poetry. I sent several rolls to Life in New York, but they wired back, ‘Who the hell is Marilyn Monroe?’”

Photographs taken later in the 1950s and early 1960s would reveal a far more confident and overtly sensual Monroe—images that would become iconic in popular culture.

Among them is the famous 1955 photograph of a busty Monroe in a white halter dress, standing as her skirt billows upward for her role in *The Seven Year Itch*. In 1962, American photographer Bert Stern captured a tipsy, sometimes nude Monroe in a series of delicate images that would become known as “The Last Sitting.”

Monroe died about six weeks later, on August 5, 1962.

In April, Life.com released newly recovered, never-before-seen photographs of Martin Luther King Jr., taken by a *Life* photographer on the day King was assassinated at a Memphis, Tennessee, hotel in 1968.

By the time audiences remember Monroe in **“The Seven Year Itch”** — standing above a New York subway grate as her white halter dress billows into one of cinema’s most reproduced images — the Monroe persona had already been refined into legend: blonde, breathy, comic, seductive and instantly marketable.

The earlier LIFE photographs suggest something less polished and more searching. Clark’s images show Monroe in a quieter register, before the full machinery of celebrity fixed her in place. She is playful, but not yet imprisoned by playfulness; glamorous, but not yet reduced to glamour.

That tension is part of why unpublished or rarely seen Monroe photographs continue to fascinate. They seem to promise access to the person behind the performance — even as they remind viewers how carefully that performance was being constructed.

### The LIFE archive keeps yielding surprises

LIFE’s photo archive has long been one of the richest visual records of 20th-century fame, politics and everyday life. In recent years, previously unpublished or overlooked images from its holdings have offered new glimpses of major cultural figures, from Hollywood stars and musicians to presidents, athletes and ordinary Americans caught in extraordinary moments.

The Monroe images join a broader pattern of archive discoveries: contact sheets, unused frames, alternate portraits and outtakes that complicate familiar public images. Such finds often show icons in between official poses — rehearsing, waiting, joking, smoking, adjusting costumes or simply looking tired.

For Monroe, that in-between space is especially powerful. Her career has often been told through a handful of famous images: the subway-grate scene from **“The Seven Year Itch,”** the radiant studio portraits, the later, more fragile photographs from **“The Last Sitting,”** Bert Stern’s haunting 1962 sessions made shortly before her death. Each set of images has contributed to a different chapter of the Monroe story.

The newly uncovered LIFE material appears to belong to an earlier chapter — before the mythology hardened, before the sadness of the final portraits, before Monroe became a symbol onto which generations projected desire, vulnerability and loss.

### Marilyn Monroe, still being rediscovered

More than six decades after her death, Monroe remains unusually present in popular culture. She is endlessly referenced in fashion, film, music and photography, while new biographies and documentaries continue to revisit the gap between Norma Jeane Mortenson’s life and Marilyn Monroe’s image.

That gap is exactly where archival photographs do their work. They do not solve the mystery of Monroe, and perhaps they should not. Instead, they widen the frame.

In Ed Clark’s photographs, Monroe is not yet the woman frozen forever in a white dress, nor the ethereal figure of **“The Last Sitting.”** She is an actress on the edge of recognition, alive to the camera and already aware of its power.

The result is a reminder that even the most familiar icons can still surprise us — especially when the archive opens another box.
